blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Multiple linear regression includes two or more predictors: ŷ = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + … + bₖxₖ. Each coefficient is the expected change in the outcome for a one-unit increase in that predictor, holding the other predictors in the model constant.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Real questions involve several variables at once: age, sex, wealth and maternal education may all relate to a child’s weight. Multiple regression fits one equation with a coefficient for each, chosen by the same least-squares principle (§12.2.2). Each coefficient describes a predictor’s association with the outcome after allowing for the others. That is the “adjustment” that makes multiple regression the main statistical tool for handling measured confounding (§12.4.1).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In the clinic register, weight regressed on age and maternal education (none as reference) gives: ŷ = 8.08 + 0.151 × age + 0.39 × (primary) + 0.77 × (secondary or higher). The age coefficient, 0.151 kg per month, now compares children of the same maternal-education group. It is almost the same as the simple-regression slope (0.150), so maternal education does not distort the age–weight association in these data.

points.html: The same LINE assumptions apply (§12.3), plus one new concern: predictors that are strongly correlated with each other (multicollinearity, §12.4.4).
R² now gives the proportion of variation explained by all predictors together; use adjusted R² (§12.2.5).
Degrees of freedom for each coefficient’s t-test are n − k − 1.

blocks.html: Confounding and Adjustment

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Adjustment means including a potential confounder as an additional predictor, so that the exposure’s coefficient estimates its association with the outcome among people with the same value of the confounder.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Recall §11.6: a confounder is associated with the exposure, affects the outcome, and is not on the causal path between them. It can create or distort an apparent relationship. Including it in the model compares like with like: the exposure coefficient is estimated within levels of the confounder, as a stratified analysis does (recall §11.7), but for many strata and continuous confounders at once.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Recall the radio-ownership example of §11.6, with household wealth as the confounder. A regression of child nutritional status on radio ownership alone shows a strong association, because wealthier households both own radios and feed children better. In predicted nutritional status = b₀ + b₁ × radio + b₂ × wealth, b₁ compares households of similar wealth, and the spurious part of the association is removed.

points.html: Regression adjusts only for confounders that were measured, measured well, and entered in the right form. An unmeasured confounder is untouched; a crudely measured or dichotomised one leaves residual confounding (recall §11.6, which separates it from unmeasured confounding; §12.4.5 shows an example). Design-stage alternatives (restriction, matching, stratification) are compared in §15.3.

Adjustment can change a coefficient’s size, significance or direction. A large change is consistent with confounding but does not prove it: chance and model specification can also shift a coefficient. In logistic regression, an odds ratio can change on adjustment even with no confounding at all, a property called non-collapsibility (§13.2.5, adjusted odds ratios). Which variables are confounders is decided from subject-matter knowledge of the causal structure (recall §11.6.1, causal diagrams), not from the size of the shift.
Do not adjust for a variable on the causal path (a mediator): that removes part of the effect you want to estimate.

blocks.html: Interpreting Multivariable Coefficients

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: In a multiple regression, each coefficient is the expected difference in the outcome per one-unit difference in that predictor, holding the other predictors in the model constant.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The qualifier is part of the result. Dropping it makes an adjusted finding sound like a bigger, simpler claim than it is.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: From §12.4: “a one-month increase in age is associated with 0.151 kg higher weight (95% CI 0.131 to 0.170), holding maternal education constant” is complete. “Age increases weight by 0.15 kg” drops the adjustment, drops the units of the predictor, and turns an association into an effect.

points.html: Always add “adjusting for …”, “holding … constant” or “controlling for …” when reporting a multivariable coefficient.
A coefficient depends on which other predictors are in the model. There is no single “effect of age”: there is the age coefficient adjusted for a stated set of variables.
For a categorical predictor, the coefficient is the difference from the reference category, holding the other predictors constant; always name the reference (§12.4.3).

blocks.html: Categorical Predictors and Interaction

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A categorical predictor with k categories enters a model as k − 1 dummy variables (each coded 0/1), with the omitted category as the reference. An interaction term, the product of two predictors, lets the effect of one predictor differ by the level of the other; this is the regression form of effect modification (recall §11.7).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Categorical predictors. A binary predictor is simple: code it 0/1, and its coefficient is the difference in mean outcome between the two groups, holding other predictors constant. With male = 0 and female = 1, the coefficient reads “average difference for girls compared with boys”.

For more than two categories, create one dummy per category except one. With four socioeconomic classes you create three dummies; the fourth is the reference, and every coefficient compares with it. One category must be left out because a fourth dummy would be redundant: someone not in classes 1, 2 or 3 must be in class 4 (an extreme case of the redundancy problem of §12.4.4).

Changing the reference category changes every coefficient in that set but leaves the fitted values unchanged. It is a reporting choice. Choose a reference that makes comparisons interpretable, such as the largest group or a natural baseline.

Interaction. A model without interaction forces a predictor to have one effect for everybody. A nutrition supplement might help malnourished children substantially and well-nourished children hardly at all. The interaction model

ŷ = b₀ + b₁(supplement) + b₂(malnourished) + b₃(supplement × malnourished)

allows this. b₁ is the supplement’s effect in the reference group only (well-nourished children), and b₃ is how much that effect changes in malnourished children, whose supplement effect is b₁ + b₃. Once an interaction is in the model, b₁ is no longer “the effect of the supplement”; reporting it as such misreads the output.

Interaction and confounding are distinct. Confounding is a distortion you adjust away to recover the association you want. Effect modification is a finding: the association really differs between groups, and you report it. One variable can be both. Interaction also depends on the scale: effects that add up exactly on the kilogram (additive) scale can show interaction on a ratio (multiplicative) scale, and vice versa, which is why interaction should be reported on both scales (Knol & VanderWeele, 2012). In linear regression the interaction term measures departure from additivity; §13.2.5 takes up the multiplicative scale of logistic regression.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
A model of child weight with socioeconomic class (four categories, class 1 as reference) and sex (illustrative numbers):

Predictor Coefficient 95% CI Interpretation
Class 2 +0.42 0.10 to 0.74 0.42 kg heavier than class 1, adjusting for sex
Class 3 +0.88 0.55 to 1.21 0.88 kg heavier than class 1, adjusting for sex
Class 4 +1.35 0.98 to 1.72 1.35 kg heavier than class 1, adjusting for sex
Female −0.31 −0.55 to −0.07 0.31 kg lighter than boys, adjusting for class

There is no “class 1” row, because class 1 is the baseline built into the intercept. To compare class 3 with class 2, subtract: 0.88 − 0.42 = 0.46 kg. Its CI and test need the model refitted with class 2 as reference (or the covariance of the two coefficients).

Now add an interaction between supplementation and baseline malnutrition, with b₁ (supplement) = +0.20 and b₃ (supplement × malnourished) = +0.75. The supplement raises weight by 0.20 kg in well-nourished children and by 0.20 + 0.75 = 0.95 kg in malnourished children. Reporting only “the supplement increases weight by 0.20 kg” would understate its effect nearly fivefold in the group that most needs it.

blocks.alt: An interaction: the supplement’s effect differs by baseline status
blocks.caption: Figure 12.4. An interaction: mean weight rises by 0.20 kg with the supplement in well-nourished children and by 0.95 kg in malnourished children. Non-parallel lines are the picture of an interaction.

points.html: k categories need k − 1 dummies. The omitted category is the reference, absorbed into the intercept. State the reference whenever you report a categorical coefficient.
Changing the reference changes coefficients, not the fit or the predictions.
An interaction term is the product of two predictors; its coefficient is how much one predictor’s effect changes across levels of the other.
With an interaction in the model, the main-effect coefficients apply only at the reference level of the other variable. Reading them as overall effects is an easy and serious misreading.
Specify interactions in advance, for a substantive reason. Testing every possible interaction until one is significant is a multiple-comparisons problem (recall §9.5.3).

blocks.html: Multicollinearity

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Multicollinearity is strong correlation among the predictors in a multiple regression, which makes it hard to separate each predictor’s own contribution to the outcome.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: A multivariable coefficient uses only the part of a predictor that the other predictors do not already explain. If two predictors are highly correlated, like maternal height and maternal weight, little independent information is left in either once the other is in the model. The two compete to explain the same shared variation.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Entering both maternal height and maternal weight as predictors of birthweight, when height and weight are strongly correlated, makes it hard to say which is more strongly related to birthweight. Their coefficients have large SEs and may take unexpected signs, even though the model as a whole predicts birthweight well.

points.html: Symptoms: unexpectedly large SEs, counterintuitive or unstable signs, and coefficients that change a lot when a minor variable is added or removed.
Multicollinearity does not bias predictions or R². It makes the individual coefficients of the correlated predictors imprecise.
It is diagnosed with the variance inflation factor (§12.4.4.1).

blocks.html: Variance Inflation Factor

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The variance inflation factor (VIF) of a predictor is how many times larger the variance of its coefficient is than it would be if that predictor were uncorrelated with the other predictors: VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − R²ⱼ), where R²ⱼ comes from regressing predictor j on all the other predictors.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: If the other predictors explain none of predictor j (R²ⱼ = 0), VIF = 1: no inflation. If they explain 80% of it, only 20% of its variation is left to estimate its coefficient from, and the variance is 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5 times larger. The SE grows by √VIF.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
With maternal height and weight in the same birthweight model, suppose the other predictors explain 78% of maternal weight: VIF = 1 ÷ 0.22 = 4.5. The variance of the maternal-weight coefficient is 4.5 times what it would be without that correlation, and its SE √4.5 = 2.1 times larger.

In the §12.6 clinic study (the analysis journey: 240 children, weight on wealth, age and sex), wealth and age correlate only weakly (r = 0.16), and every VIF is 1.03 or less.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
m  <- read.csv("data/journey_mlr.csv")
m$sex <- factor(m$sex, levels = c("M", "F"))
fm <- lm(weight_kg ~ wealth_index + age_months + sex, data = m)
library(car)
vif(fm)
cor(m$wealth_index, m$age_months, use = "complete.obs")
wealth_index   age_months          sex 
    1.025452     1.027001     1.001543 
[1] 0.1575423

With one other continuous predictor, R²ⱼ is close to r² = 0.158² = 0.025, so VIF ≈ 1 ÷ 0.975 = 1.03, as printed. The wealth coefficient’s SE is inflated by only √1.03 ≈ 1.01.

points.html: VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − R²ⱼ). The minimum is 1; there is no upper limit.

Cut-offs of 5 or 10 are conventions, not laws. The “rule of 10” is widely used, but a VIF of 10 or more does not by itself discredit a regression or require dropping a variable (O’Brien, 2007). What matters is whether the coefficient of interest is precise enough for the question, which its CI shows directly.

Remedies, when the imprecision matters: drop one of two predictors that measure the same thing, combine them into a single index, or use principal components (§16.5: new uncorrelated variables built as weighted sums of the originals). High VIF in adjustment covariates that are not of interest usually needs no remedy.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 12.4

questions.prompt: Household wealth and household electricity access are strongly correlated. In a model containing both, each has a wide CI and neither is significant, though R² is high. What is the likely explanation, and how would you confirm it?
questions.answer: Multicollinearity. The two predictors share most of their variation, so the model cannot separate their individual contributions: each coefficient’s SE is inflated, though together they explain the outcome well (hence the high R²). Confirm with the variance inflation factor (VIF): large VIFs for both, and a large R²ⱼ when one is regressed on the other. A joint F-test of the two (the nested-model F-test taught later, in §12.4.5) would be significant even though neither t-test is.

questions.prompt: A crude regression coefficient for a drug’s effect is 0.90, and the coefficient adjusted for age is 0.35. What does this comparison show, and what does it not show?
questions.answer: It shows that age accounts for a large part of the crude association, which is consistent with age confounding the drug–outcome relationship (for example, if older patients both received the drug more often and had higher outcome values). It does not by itself prove confounding: the shift could partly reflect chance or model specification, and whether age is a confounder (associated with drug use, affecting the outcome, not on the causal path) must be argued from subject-matter knowledge before fitting. The adjusted 0.35 also remains open to confounding by unmeasured variables.

questions.prompt: In a model with an interaction, b₁ (supplement) = 0.30 kg and b₃ (supplement × malnourished) = 0.50 kg. What is the supplement’s estimated effect in malnourished children? Separately: regressing one predictor on the others gives R²ⱼ = 0.75. What is its VIF, and by what factor is its SE inflated?
questions.answer: Effect in malnourished children = b₁ + b₃ = 0.30 + 0.50 = 0.80 kg (0.30 kg applies only to well-nourished children, the reference group). VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.75) = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4. The variance of that coefficient is 4 times what it would be without the correlation, so the SE is √4 = 2 times larger.

blocks.html: Non-Linear Relationships – Categories, Trend Tests and Splines

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A continuous predictor need not enter a model as a straight line. It can enter as categories (dummy variables for ranges of values), as a score for ordered categories (a test for linear trend), or as a spline: a smooth curve built from pieces joined at chosen values called knots. A restricted cubic spline uses cubic pieces between the knots and is constrained to be a straight line beyond the outer knots.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
The linearity assumption (§12.3) says each extra unit of x adds the same amount to y. Three tools relax or test that:

  • Categories make no assumption about shape: each group gets its own mean. The price is several coefficients, and the assumption that the outcome is flat within each group and jumps at the boundaries.
  • A trend test gives ordered categories the scores 1, 2, 3, … and fits one slope across them: one coefficient, testing whether the outcome rises steadily across the ordered groups (recall the chi-square test for trend, §10.6.5, the same idea for proportions). Comparing the trend model with the category model tests departure from a straight-line trend.
  • A spline follows a smooth curve using a few extra coefficients. With 4 knots, a restricted cubic spline uses 3 coefficients instead of 1. The knots are usually placed at fixed centiles of x; for 4 knots, Harrell’s defaults are the 5th, 35th, 65th and 95th centiles (Harrell, 2015). Comparing the spline with the straight line tests non-linearity.

Do not dichotomise a continuous predictor. Splitting age at 24 months, or BMI at 25, throws information away. It assumes every child just below the cut-off is like the youngest child, and every child just above it is like the oldest. Dichotomising loses power, creates residual confounding when the variable is a confounder, and a cut-point chosen by looking at the data biases the results (Royston, Altman & Sauerbrei, 2006). Keep the variable continuous, and use a spline if the shape is in doubt. Report categories, if clinically useful, as a description alongside the continuous analysis.

Derivation (the F-test comparing nested models)

  1. A smaller model (straight-line trend) is nested in a larger one (categories) when setting some of the larger model’s coefficients to fixed values gives the smaller.
  2. The larger model never has a larger SSE. The question is whether the drop, SSE_small − SSE_large, is bigger than chance would give for the extra q coefficients.
  3. F = [(SSE_small − SSE_large) ÷ q] ÷ [SSE_large ÷ df_large]: the drop per extra coefficient, divided by the residual variance of the larger model.
  4. Under H₀ (the smaller model is adequate), F follows the F-distribution on (q, df_large) degrees of freedom (recall §5.7.2.5). With q = 1, F = t², as in §12.2.5.

Illustration / Example: Worked Calculation (clinic register, wealth quintile 1 = poorest, adjusted for age)

  1. Categories. With quintile 1 as reference, the age-adjusted coefficients are 0.36, 0.70, 1.11 and 1.62 kg for quintiles 2 to 5. The steps (0.36, 0.34, 0.41, 0.51 kg) are roughly equal, so the pattern looks like a straight-line trend.
  2. Trend. Entering quintile as the score 1 to 5 gives 0.40 kg per quintile (SE 0.048, t = 8.35, p < 0.001): weight rises steadily with wealth.
  3. Departure from trend. SSE is 39.46 for the trend model (97 df) and 39.26 for the category model (94 df), so q = 3. F = [(39.46 − 39.26) ÷ 3] ÷ (39.26 ÷ 94) = 0.067 ÷ 0.418 = 0.16, p = 0.92. No evidence that a straight-line trend is inadequate, so the one-coefficient trend model is the better summary.
  4. Spline for age. A 4-knot restricted cubic spline (knots at 12, 20.65, 29 and 36 months) lowers SSE from 67.81 to 66.61 at a cost of 2 coefficients. F = (1.20 ÷ 2) ÷ (66.61 ÷ 96) = 0.87, p = 0.42. The straight line for age is adequate in these data.
  5. Cost of dichotomising age. Splitting age at 24 months drops R² from 0.67 to 0.49, and the residual SD rises from 0.83 to 1.03 kg. Four age groups recover R² = 0.68, but only by spending 3 coefficients on a step-shaped curve.
  6. Residual confounding. In the §12.6 study, the wealth coefficient adjusted for age as a continuous variable is 0.62 kg. Adjusted for age split at 24 months it is 0.70 kg: the split leaves part of age’s confounding in place.

blocks.alt: Four ways to model age: split at 24 months, quartile groups, straight line and restricted cubic spline
blocks.caption: Figure 12.5. Weight on age in the clinic register, with age entered four ways. The split at 24 months (R² = 0.49) forces a jump at the cut-off and flat lines on either side. Quartile groups (0.68) and the spline (0.68) spend 3 coefficients each and follow the straight line (0.67), which is the adequate model here.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(rms))    # for rcs()
cl <- read.csv("data/clinic_children.csv")
fcat <- lm(weight_kg ~ age_months + factor(wealth_quintile),
           data = cl)
ftr  <- lm(weight_kg ~ age_months + wealth_quintile, data = cl)
round(summary(fcat)$coef, 3)
round(summary(ftr)$coef, 3)
anova(ftr, fcat)                 # departure from linear trend
flin <- lm(weight_kg ~ age_months, data = cl)
fspl <- lm(weight_kg ~ rcs(age_months, 4), data = cl)
anova(flin, fspl)                # is the spline better than the line?

Model 2: weight_kg ~ age_months + factor(wealth_quintile)

Model 1: weight_kg ~ age_months
Model 2: weight_kg ~ rcs(age_months, 4)
  Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F Pr(>F)

factor() makes the four dummies of step 1, each against quintile 1. Without factor(), the quintile enters as the score 1–5 and gives the single trend slope of step 2. The first anova is the F-test of step 3 (RSS is R’s name for SSE); the second compares the spline with the straight line (step 4). splines::ns(age_months, df = 3) fits a similar natural spline without the rms package.

points.html: Keep continuous predictors continuous. Dichotomising loses power, leaves residual confounding, and a data-driven cut-point biases the estimate (Royston, Altman & Sauerbrei, 2006).

Categories make no shape assumption but assume a flat outcome within each group. Fix the cut-points in advance (for example, quintiles or clinical bands), never by searching for the most significant split.
Test for trend: code ordered categories 1, 2, 3, … and test the single slope. Test for departure from trend: F-test of the category model against the trend model.

Restricted cubic splines model a smooth curve with k − 1 coefficients for k knots, linear beyond the outer knots; 3 to 5 knots at fixed centiles is the usual convention (Harrell, 2015). A spline coefficient has no simple interpretation: present the fitted curve as a plot.

A non-significant test of non-linearity supports keeping the straight line; it does not prove the true relationship is linear. Choosing between linear, categorical and spline forms by repeated testing is itself a multiplicity problem; §15.1.5 (modelling strategy, how the aim of the model governs these choices) returns to this.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 12.5

questions.prompt: A study reports “children with maternal BMI ≥ 25 had 0.4 kg higher birthweight (p = 0.04)”, after the authors tried cut-offs of 22, 23, 24, 25 and 26. Give two reasons this analysis is weak, and say how you would reanalyse it.
questions.answer: 1. Dichotomising a continuous predictor discards information and power, and treats a mother at BMI 25.1 like one at 35. (ii) The cut-off was chosen as the most significant of five tries, a multiple-comparisons problem that biases the estimate away from zero and inflates the false-positive rate; p = 0.04 after five looks is weak evidence. Reanalyse with maternal BMI continuous, checking the shape with a restricted cubic spline (3–4 knots at fixed centiles) and testing non-linearity by comparing spline and straight-line models; present the fitted curve with its CI band. Categories fixed in advance may be added as a description.

questions.prompt: Adding three dummy variables for four categories to a trend model lowers SSE from 52.0 to 50.5. The category model has 120 residual df. Compute F for departure from a linear trend and say whether it suggests the trend model is inadequate (the 5% critical value of F on 3 and 120 df is 2.68).
questions.answer: F = [(52.0 − 50.5) ÷ 3] ÷ (50.5 ÷ 120) = 0.50 ÷ 0.421 = 1.19. This is below 2.68 (p > 0.05), so there is no evidence of departure from a straight-line trend; the one-coefficient trend model is the better summary. (No evidence of departure is not proof that the trend is exactly linear.)
